Chick Flick
CHIK flik
noun (Gen X slang)
Chick for a young woman is American slang of the 1920s (from chicken, a young person); flick for a motion picture is of the same decade, from the flicker of early film. The rhyming compound chick flick was in American use by the late 1980s and in everyone’s mouth by the early 1990s, attached to romances and tearjerkers marketed chiefly to women: Beaches (1988), Steel Magnolias (1989), Sleepless in Seattle (1993). It was usually said by a husband or boyfriend, with a sigh, on the way into the theater.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A chick flick is a movie made for women — romance, tears, friendship, a wedding near the end — and the word is usually said by a husband with a sigh as he is led to one. The phrase is half joke and half complaint, and it tells the truth about something: the film industry learned to sell longing. The Christian observation is that the longing is not the problem. God made it. The Song of Solomon is the Bible’s own love song, and it says "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it" (Son 8:7). What Scripture adds is order and patience: "stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Son 2:7). Desire is a fire for the hearth of marriage, not a thing to be fanned for an evening’s entertainment. The danger of a steady diet of screen romance is that it trains a girl to wait for a script and a boy to think love is a feeling that happens to people rather than a covenant men keep. The Bible’s love story is better than Hollywood’s: "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it" (Eph 5:25). Real love "suffereth long, and is kind" (1Co 13:4); it can still "rejoice with the wife of thy youth" (Pro 5:18) forty years after the credits. A father can watch the movie with his daughter and then tell her the truth: the best love story is not the one where a stranger sweeps you off your feet, but the one where a man lays down his life for his bride — the story Christ wrote first.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen X slang (late 1980s–90s) for a romantic film marketed to women; Scripture honors the longing — many waters cannot quench love (Son 8:7) — and shows its true shape in a husband who gives himself as Christ did (Eph 5:25).

CHICK FLICK, n. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s, American) A motion picture, usually a romance or tearjerker, made and marketed chiefly for women. "You picked last time — no more chick flicks."

Rhyming compound of chick (a young woman, 1920s slang) and flick (a film, 1920s, from the flicker of early projection).

Counterparts: guy movie, dude flick; kin to tearjerker, weepie, rom-com.

Webster 1828: CHICKEN, n. 1. The young of fowls, particularly of the domestic hen, or gallinaceous fowls. 2. A person of tender years. …

Decode for parents: the longing these films sell is real and God-given; teach children that love is a covenant kept, not a feeling that happens to them.

Key Scripture

Son 8:7 — "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned."

Son 2:7 — "I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please."

Eph 5:25 — "Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;"

1Co 13:4 — "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,"

Pro 5:18 — "Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth."

Modern Corruption

The chick flick sells a real, God-given longing in a script that ends at the wedding; Scripture shows love as a covenant kept long after the credits roll.

expand to see more

Romance as a product. Hollywood discovered that longing could be packaged, and the result was a genre that wakes desire on a schedule: two hours of stirring up, a kiss, the credits. The Shulamite’s refrain runs the other way — "stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please" (Son 2:7). A girl fed on the formula can come to measure a real husband against a scripted one and find him dull; a boy can conclude that love is lightning rather than labor. Neither lesson is in the Song of Solomon.

The better story. Scripture does not sneer at romance; it puts a whole love song in the canon (Son 8:7). But it finishes the story Hollywood stops telling: the husband who loves his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it (Eph 5:25), the charity that suffereth long (1Co 13:4), the man who still rejoices with the wife of his youth (Pro 5:18) when both are gray. The sneer in the name — that such stories are only for women — misses the point too: covenant love is a man’s work first.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Chicken → 1920s chick (young woman) + 1920s flick (film) → chick flick (late 1980s–90s romances); Scripture: love that many waters cannot quench, kept in covenant (Son 8:7; Eph 5:25).

1920s American slang: chick, a young woman; the flicks, the movies

Scripture’s love story: the Song of Solomon (Son 8:7) and Christ and His church (Eph 5:25)
